2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the appellants as pre-emptors filed Miscellaneous (pre-emption) Case No. 6 of 1998 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Thana Borura, District-Comilla against Abdul Hamid, the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptee-respondent Nos. 1-8 herein praying for pre-emption of the case land measuring .32 acre out of .70 acre, as fully described in the schedule to the application for pre-emption. The pre-emptors stated, inter alia, that the case land measuring .32 acre along with the remaining land measuring .38 acre of the disputed Dag Nos. 189-193 and khatian No.208 originally belonged to Sridam Chandra Mazumder and his name was correctly recorded in the Khatian. After his death his only son Surya Kumar Mazumder, opposite party No. 2 (in the miscellaneous case), became the owner and, thereafter, he gifted .40 acre of land therefrom to his wife-Sagori Rani by a deed of gift dated 16.11.1991 and she thereafter sold the same to the pre-emptor No. 1 by a deed of sale dated 02.1.2003 and put him in possession. The opposite party No. 2 sold .041/2 acre of land from plot No. 168 and .28 acre of land from plot No. 185 in total .321/2 acre by a deed dated 24.1.1993. He also sold .42 acre of land from plot No. 184 to the pre-emptors by a deed dated 20.4.1993. In this way the pre-emptors became co-sharers in the disputed S.A. Khatian No.208 by purchase. The vendor-opposite party No. 2 sold the case land to the pre-emptee by a deed of sale dated 25.9.1994 without serving a notice upon the pre-emptors, who are co-sharers in the disputed jote. 

 14. It is true that the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction cannot reassess the evidence on record and should not readily reverse the concurrent findings of fact of the trial Court and the appellate Court which are both Courts of fact. However, it is within the jurisdiction of the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction to see whether the trial Court and the appellate Court have misread or left out of consideration any evidence on record. We should mention at the outset that the learned Advocate for the respondents pointed out from a copy of the khatian-Exhibit-‘cha', that it shows Abdul Hamid as one of the owners in plot No.264. Therefore, the finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court that Abdul Hamid did not own any land in plot No.264 is not a correct appreciation of the record. 

 15. The learned Advocate for the respondents by reference to a decision in the case of Feroza Majid and another Vs. Jiban Bima Corporation reported in 39 DLR (AD)78, submitted that when the document itself mentions in the recital that it is a deed of exchange, no oral evidence can be led to disprove such term of the agreement. He submitted that sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act preclude any oral evidence to contradict the terms of the contract detailed in the written document. We also took a similar view in the unreported decision in the case of Md. Shahed Ali Vs. Abdul Hafiz in Civil Appeal No.10 of 2009, wherein three of us were party and judgment was delivered on 19.07.2017. This Division held that when the transaction between the parties was reduced to writing and registered in accordance with law, the deed itself is proof of its content, i.e. that it is a deed of exchange. However, in that case we observed that only evidence relating to allegation of fraud, intimidation, illegality, want of due execution, want of capacity in any contracting party, want or failure of consideration or mistake in fact or law can be proved by adducing oral evidence. To that extent in a case for pre-emption evidence may be led to prove that the trans-action described as an exchange was in essence a sham or colourable transaction. However, in the facts of the instant case, we are of the view that the value of the land shown in the deed as Tk.4000/- does not indicate that the sum of money mentioned was handed over as consideration. The recital of the deed does not say that the sum of money was consideration for the transaction. The amount is merely mentioned as the value of the land. We also note that the main reason given by the appellate Court for not accepting the transaction as exchange, was the notion that Abdul Hamid did not have title in plot No. 264 and, therefore, he could not legally exchange land of that plot and, hence, the exchange was a sham or colourable transaction. In this regard, we have noted above that the Khatian which was shown to us indicates that Abdul Hamid did have interest in plot No. 264, and hence, the finding of the trial Court and appellate Court is not sustainable.
